rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pretemporal covenant was made with every human being, so no one can claim on Judgment Day to have merely inherited ancestral idolatry.
rows.anchor: the pretemporal covenant was also made with all, and not some, human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quranic narratives show people using ancestral practice to resist prophetic warnings; the Quran mocks and rejects this excuse.
rows.anchor: In several Quranic accounts, people reject their prophets’ warnings against idolatry and sin by arguing that they are following the practices of their fathers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ancestral excuse cannot stand because all people received innate understanding of religious truth and God's sole Lordship through the covenant with Adam and his progeny.
rows.anchor: God has endowed all human beings, by virtue of the pretemporal covenant made with Adam and all his progeny

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This teaching connects with Islamic tradition's broad disparagement of blind imitation of other people's religious views.
rows.anchor: This basic Quranic teaching is connected to the widespread disparaging in Islamic tradition of “blind imitation,” or taqlīd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqlīd is permissible in legal details without innate moral or spiritual basis and in following the Prophet's Sunnah, but not in fundamental beliefs, which require personal understanding as far as possible.
rows.anchor: Taqlīd is considered permissible regarding matters of religious Law that are not based necessarily upon an innate moral or spiritual understanding

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's question resembles Moses' plea in verse 155, which asks God not to destroy the people for what their fools did.
rows.anchor: Wilt Thou destroy us for that which the falsifiers have done? is similar in form to Moses’ plea

rows.speaker: many Ashʿarites
rows.claim: They read “created for Hell” literally: God created some jinn and humans with an innate inclination toward acts that inevitably lead to perdition.
rows.anchor: For many Ashʿarites, the verse should be read literally to mean that God created certain human beings and jinn in such a way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal interpretation accords with verses in which God guides some and misleads others.
rows.anchor: the verse is consistent with other verses indicating that God guides some and misleads others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith supports the literal reading by saying that, before birth, God tells an angel to record a person's provision, lifespan, works, and blissful or wretched fate.
rows.anchor: one that indicates that while the child is still unborn, God commands an angel to write down his or her worldly provision, life span, works, and fate as either blissful or wretched in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: Muʿtazilites and many others
rows.claim: They understand God as foreknowing individuals' moral choices and destinies without determining them.
rows.anchor: Muʿtazilites and many others, however, read the verse to mean that God has foreknowledge of individuals’ moral choices and destinies, but does not determine them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One possible reading treats “created for Hell” as describing the many jinn and humans' eventual destination there.
rows.anchor: The statement that He created them for Hell may simply be meant to indicate their final end

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possible reading says some disbelievers are so entrenched that it is as though they were created for Hell.
rows.anchor: it may express the idea that some jinn and men are so deeply entrenched in disbelief that it is as if they were created for Hell

rows.speaker: Muʿtazilites
rows.claim: They reject literal creation for disobedience because it would impose commands on people innately unable to fulfill them, making the commands futile, unjust, and unmerciful.
rows.anchor: God has given certain individuals moral commands that they are innately incapable of fulfilling, something that would be futile, unjust, and unmerciful

rows.speaker: Muʿtazilites
rows.claim: They also argue that the literal reading conflicts with the statement that jinn and humankind were created to worship God.
rows.anchor: a literal reading of this verse would conflict with a literal reading of other verses, such as 51:56

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heart, understood as the seat of understanding, intelligence, and knowledge, together with eyes and ears, forms the faculties for guidance to truth.
rows.anchor: The eyes, the ears, and the heart—the last of which is considered the seat of understanding, intelligence, and knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These faculties fail their intended function either because God seals or covers them or because people refuse to use them properly.
rows.anchor: God has “sealed” or “covered” them (see, e.g., 2:7; 47:16) or because human beings have refused to employ them properly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators say the heedless do not contemplate God's signs, His Oneness, or prophetic messages in their hearts.
rows.anchor: Their hearts do not contemplate the various signs of God and His Oneness or the messages sent through His prophets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators say their eyes fail to see the obvious signs of God's creative power in the surrounding world.
rows.anchor: their eyes do not see the obvious signs of God’s creative Power in the world around them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators say they do not hear scripture's teachings, but hear only temptation; verse 41:5 depicts their claimed deafness and veiling.
rows.anchor: their ears do not hear the teachings of the scriptures (Ṭ, Z), but only the call of temptation (Qu)

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The comparison with cattle rests on their lack of intellect for understanding religious truth.
rows.anchor: for cattle do not possess an intellect with which to understand religious truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People who fail to use their intellect are worse than beasts because they squander an intellect given for discerning truth.
rows.anchor: they are even worse for squandering the gift of intellect, which they have been given precisely for the purpose of discerning truth

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Like cattle, such people care only for base desires such as food and comfort.
rows.anchor: Like cattle, such persons are concerned only with fulfilling base desires for food and comfort

rows.speaker: Aj, R, Ṭ, and Z
rows.claim: Cattle avoid what harms them and seek nourishment, whereas disbelievers work toward spiritual destruction, making the latter even more astray.
rows.anchor: even cattle know enough to flee from what is harmful for them and to seek out what nourishes them

rows.speaker: Islamic tradition
rows.claim: Animals and natural phenomena recognize their Creator, unlike disbelievers.
rows.anchor: animals and all natural phenomena recognize their Creator, but the disbelievers do not

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cattle can be guided by a herdsman's call or shout, but disbelievers refuse guidance altogether.
rows.anchor: although cattle can be guided by the call of their herdsman, even if they hear it only as a call and a shout

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following the heedless of verse 179, the verse tells people to call upon God by His Most Beautiful Names; commentators connect the verb with supplication and remembrance of God.
rows.anchor: The verb that translates call upon also means “to supplicate” and is here connected by commentators with the practice of remembering and invoking God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is a scriptural basis for dhikr in Islamic spirituality, especially Sufism.
rows.anchor: This verse is thus one of the scriptural bases for the practice of dhikr in Islamic spirituality and especially Sufism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's Most Beautiful Names also appear in 20:8 and 59:24, while 17:110 similarly commands invocation by them.
rows.anchor: Mention of God’s Most Beautiful Names is also found in 20:8; 59:24; and a similar command to call upon them is made in 17:110

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term al-ḥusnā relates to goodness and virtue, and the Names are beautiful both to the ear and to the heart.
rows.anchor: a word also related to goodness and virtue, and are said to be beautiful to the ear as well as the heart (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A widely reported hadith underlies the traditional teaching that God has ninety-nine Beautiful Names.
rows.anchor: God is traditionally said to have ninety-nine Beautiful Names

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lists of the Names vary and may exceed ninety-nine; they are grounded in Quranic descriptions, and some derive from divine actions described there.
rows.anchor: While the list of those Names varies slightly in different reports, and several lists contain more than ninety-nine

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Names do not compromise God's Oneness or divide Him into parts; they express qualities of His undifferentiated Essence that become differentiated through self-manifestation and perceived by the caller.
rows.anchor: the Names are considered to represent Attributes or Qualities of His undifferentiated Essence, which are differentiated through the Self-manifestation of the Essence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Names reveal both essential divine attributes and the different ways God relates to creation.
rows.anchor: They also reveal different Attributes of God, some pertaining to His Essence, and others to the different ways in which He relates to His creation

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabrisī
rows.claim: Each Name has a real Divine Presence or Quality; there are no empty titles for God.
rows.anchor: as al-Ṭabrisī notes there are no empty titles for God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islamic metaphysics regards the cosmos as reflections or theophanies of the Divine Names and Qualities.
rows.anchor: the whole of the cosmos is considered to be in reality nothing but reflections or theophanies

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Names and Qualities are major concerns in theology, philosophy, and Sufism; the science of Divine Names includes al-jafr, symbolic numerology of Names and their letters.
rows.anchor: the science of Divine Names (ʿilm al-asmāʾ), which includes the science of al-jafr—that is, the science of the symbolic numerical significance

rows.speaker: most Islamic thinkers
rows.claim: They identify God's Names as Attributes, usually dividing them into Attributes of Essence and of action, while traditional sources differ on classification and on whether Attributes are distinct from or identical with Essence.
rows.anchor: Most Islamic thinkers agree that God’s Names are His Attributes

rows.speaker: Islamic esoterism
rows.claim: It regards God and His Names as one; God is present in the sanctified Names, each a ladder leading to Him.
rows.anchor: In Islamic esoterism, God and His Names are considered one

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names are also divided into those of Beauty, such as Compassionate and Merciful, and Majesty, such as Judge and Compeller.
rows.anchor: such as Compassionate, Merciful, Gentle, Kind, and Pardoner, and those of Majesty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Names can be manifested in humans while others belong to God alone; human names may use the former but not the latter, and some Names fit both categories.
rows.anchor: the Names have been also divided into those that could be manifested in human beings (Kind, Generous) and those that belong to God alone

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: One view says all God's Names are Most Beautiful; another narrows the phrase to Names of Beauty, encouraging invocation for mercy while discouraging invocation of Names of Majesty or Wrath.
rows.anchor: some suggest that here the Most Beautiful Names refers specifically to the Names of Beauty, which believers are encouraged to call upon

rows.speaker: other commentators
rows.claim: Others allow calling God by any Name or description found in the Quran, citing expressions such as completer of His Light and best of plotters.
rows.anchor: Others assert that one can call upon God by any Name or description of God found in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's supreme Name is Allāh, said to encompass all His other Names.
rows.anchor: God’s supreme Name is Allāh, which is said to encompass all of His other Names

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sufis commonly repeat Allāh or other Names prescribed by a shaykh to cultivate virtues and treat spiritual ailments, figuratively transmuting the soul from lead into gold.
rows.anchor: it is also common for them to repeatedly invoke other Divine Names under the instruction of a shaykh

rows.speaker: Sufi commentators
rows.claim: They view Quranic Names and Attributes as limits of human knowledge of God and as gates to His infinite reality, enabling knowledge beyond what is humanly accessible.
rows.anchor: but also gates to His infinite Reality and the forms made available to human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who deviate may use specifically human attributes such as father or son for God, attribute evil actions or intentions to Him, or anthropomorphize Him with ignorant or unworthy descriptions.
rows.anchor: Those who deviate with regard to His Names are said to be those who refer to Him using specifically human attributes, such as “father” or “son”

rows.speaker: several commentators
rows.claim: They say God should be named only with descriptions in the Quran or Sunnah, even when another description is synonymous with a scriptural Name.
rows.anchor: Several commentators assert that one should not refer to God using any name or description not found in the Quran or the Sunnah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ritual invocation requires Arabic, but private supplication outside canonical prayer or Sufi dhikr may use non-Arabic names such as Persian Khudā or English God.
rows.anchor: Whenever the invocation of God’s Names is done ritually, the Names have to be invoked in Arabic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deviation can mean using God's Names or their derivatives for false gods; the pagan Makkans worshipped Allāt, apparently a feminine form of Allāh.
rows.anchor: To deviate with regard to His Names can also refer to those who use His Names or derivations from them to designate false gods or idols

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Daʾb means habit, custom, or practice; some commentators say it includes both the people's habitual deeds and what befell them, namely defeat or destruction.
rows.anchor: Some commentators understand this daʾb as both what they did as a matter of habit and what happened to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Generally, God gives people intelligence, strength, free will, and life's goods so they can worship and do good; they change themselves when they turn instead to sin and unbelief.
rows.anchor: God gives human beings intelligence, strength, free will, and good things in life, so that they can worship God and do good

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: In context, the blessing may be the Quraysh's receiving a prophet from among them, whom they denied and drove out.
rows.anchor: some see this verse as referring to God’s blessing the Quraysh by sending them a prophet who was one of them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The longer account of Moses and Pharaoh appears in 7:103–136.
rows.anchor: For a longer account of the story of Moses and Pharaoh, see 7:103–36

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some think verses 128–129 were the last revealed to the Prophet before his death, though commentators substantially disagree about which passage came last.
rows.anchor: It is thought by some that vv. 128–29 were the very last to be revealed to the Prophet before his death

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: They take “from among your own” as reminding Arabs of the blessing of a prophet from their community who spoke their language.
rows.anchor: others understand your own to mean humanity as such

rows.speaker: other commentators
rows.claim: Others understand “your own” to refer to humanity as such.
rows.anchor: others understand your own to mean humanity as such

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some cite the Prophet's noble lineage, tracing it back to Abraham, when explaining his being from among his own.
rows.anchor: the significance of the lineage of the Prophet, in particular that he comes from a noble line going all the way back to Abraham

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others say the Arabs remain elevated because the Prophet was one of them.
rows.anchor: the Arabs were and still are elevated by the fact that the Prophet was one of them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's concern means he is anxious that people avoid the Fire and find guidance, and hopeful that they enter the Garden.
rows.anchor: he is anxious for them not to enter the Fire, to be guided and find the right way

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: They note that the Prophet is honored here with qualities usually attributed to God in the Quran, as in the description of God as kind and merciful to humankind.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is honored here by qualities usually attributable to God in the Quran

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Supplication here means magnification and praise.
rows.anchor: supplication in this context is understood to mean a form of magnification and praise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Peace, a common Muslim greeting in this life, is also Paradise's greeting and is heard there from God and angels; Paradise is called the Abode of Peace.
rows.anchor: Peace, which is the common greeting among Muslims in this world, is also the greeting among the people of Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The coming of God's command and the oven's gushing mark the flood's beginning, sent to destroy Noah's people.
rows.anchor: indicates the beginning of the flood, which God sent to destroy the people of Noah

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The oven is understood as the earth in general or as a particular region, such as Syria or Iraq.
rows.anchor: The oven here refers to the earth (Bg, Q) in general or a particular region, such as Syria or Iraq (Bg)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of the oven gushing forth is discussed further at 23:27–28.
rows.anchor: for more on the oven gushed forth, see 23:27–28c

rows.speaker: one account
rows.claim: God gathered all kinds of birds and animals before Noah, who selected one male and one female of each species for the ship.
rows.anchor: According to one account, God first gathered all manner of birds and animals before Noah, who then chose one male and one female from each species

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception for those already condemned includes both Noah's wife and his son.
rows.anchor: save the one against whom the Word has already gone forth characterizes both Noah’s wife (see 66:10c) and his son

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses narrative is also told in several other Quranic passages.
rows.anchor: For the story of Moses, see also 2:49–61; 7:103–55; 10:75–93

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs Moses brought, also called clear proofs, were his miracles.
rows.anchor: The signs with which Moses came, which are also referred to as clear proofs (7:105; 29:39), are the miracles he performed (Kl)

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some identify the manifest authority given to Moses as his staff.
rows.anchor: Some state that a manifest authority refers to Moses’staff specifically (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For discussion of Pharaoh's notables, the commentary points to 7:103 and 10:75.
rows.anchor: On the notables of Pharaoh, see 7:103c; 10:75c

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The word wird usually evokes quenching thirst, intensifying the severity of Pharaoh's people's punishment.
rows.anchor: Watering place renders wird, a word usually associated with the quenching of thirst

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh leads his people to Hell at the Resurrection in accordance with the verse saying every people will be called by its imam.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh’s people will be led by him to Hell on the Day of Resurrection in accordance with 17:71

rows.speaker: Z and Ṭ
rows.claim: The curse pursuing Pharaoh's people in this world may be a general curse or specifically their drowning in the Red Sea.
rows.anchor: can refer to a curse in general (Z) or specifically to their being drowned in the Red Sea (Ṭ; see 7:136c).
